newsitem.title: USA: U.S. prepares response to Iraq attack on Kurds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. prepares response to Iraq attack on Kurds.

text.p: The State Department on Monday night urged all American citizens to leave Iraq as indications grew that President Bill Clinton had approved plans to launch a U.S. military strike against Iraq.

Clinton returned to Washington from a campaign trip amid reports that a cruise missile strike against Iraqi military targets could be imminent in retaliation for a massive attack by Iraqi troops against Kurds in northern Iraq.

The United States stationed warships armed with accurate Tomahawk cruise missiles in the Gulf and moved B-52 bombers carrying air-launched cruise missiles to Guam in the Pacific. The B-52s can fly non-stop into missile range several hundred miles from Iraq.
The $1.2 million ship-launched Tomahawks can fly unmanned nearly 700 miles (1,120 km) and strike targets.
The United States said Iraqi troops appeared to be moving deeper into Kurdish opposition-held territory in northern Iraq, and that Clinton had readied a "course of action" in response.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, speaking to reporters in Milwaukee where Clinton made an earlier campaign appearance, refused to confirm reports that Clinton had signed off on military action, but said that "clearly political, economic and military aspects have been under consideration."
U.S. officials said Iraq's President Saddam Hussein must be made to pay for ignoring U.S. warnings against attacking Kurds north of the 36th parallel in his country.
McCurry told reporters there was evidence that some of the Iraqi forces that overran the Kurdish stronghold of Arbil over the weekend were "penetrating deeper" into northern Iraq.
The State Department urged all American citizens to leave Iraq, citing "soaring violence" in the north and Baghdad's "renewed campaign of repression."

"The U.S. government views with grave concern the latest reports of soaring violence in northern Iraq. Given the government of Iraq's renewed campaign of repression, it is strongly recommended that all U.S. citizens leave Iraq," the department said.
The written statement said the U.S. government was contacting private organisations that had Americans in northern Iraq to urge that they be withdrawn immediately.
Two members of the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee said in an appearance on CNN on Monday they expected U.S. military action.
Democratic Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said the most likely target for a U.S. strike was Iraqi military facilities.
"It should be tough," Lieberman said. "There should be no doubt in Saddam's mind that the military has to pay."
Republican Sen. William Cohen said, "I would think it would come ... on command-and-control facilities closer to Baghdad rather than in the Kurdish areas."

The White House believes Saddam sent three tank divisions composed of 30,000-40,000 elite Republican Guard troops into northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction involved in a bloody power struggle with another Kurdish group with links to Iran.
It says U.N. Security Council resolutions approved after a U.S.-led coalition defeated Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War provide the legal basis for responding to Saddam's actions.
The Iraqi military advance threatened the town of Sulaymaniyah, the administrative capital of the Kurdish opposition, McCurry said earlier.

"There was, you know, some discussions about redeploying his units outside the town of Arbil. Some of that did happen although they remained in firm control of the area. There is other evidence that he (Saddam) is using some of that force to penetrate deeper into Kurdish-occupied territories in northern Iraq," he added.

Clinton, who placed U.S. forces in the Gulf region on high alert on Saturday, had defined "a course of action and has been consulting some governments and informing some governments of that course of action," McCurry said.
In 1993 Clinton launched a missile attack on Iraq in response to its alleged plot to assassinate former President George Bush while Bush was visiting Kuwait that year.
The missiles destroyed an Iraqi intelligence headquarters in Baghdad where U.S. officials said the plot was hatched.
CNN, citing a Pentagon source, reported that U.S. Air Force B-52 bombers carrying cruise missiles had taken off from Guam, but it was unknown if they were headed for Iraq.
Asked about the report, McCurry noted that B-52s were long-range aircraft, adding: "I don't know that that would be particularly significant."
